extracted.intended_audience: newspaper sports reporters and editors (aspiring and practicing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and structuring sports news stories for newspapers, including ethics, leads, analysis, box scores, and department practices. Focuses on how to write for diverse audiences and the practical constraints of newspapers and compositors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectional-story paragraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: So far as he possibly can, he makes each paragraph a block or entity, to minimize the damage that may come if the composing room assembles the sections in wrong sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid linking paragraphs with transitional words like 'Meanwhile' or 'However' in sectional stories. Make paragraphs self-contained blocks so sections can be rearranged without destroying sense. Also ensure each fragment/section is identified with the same slugline and given its proper number in the sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slugline/section identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Every section must be identified with the same slugline and that each fragment must be given its proper number in the sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing sectional stories, consistently use the same slugline for each section and number fragments so compositors can assemble them correctly; failure to do so risks mis-assembly by the composing room or apprentices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting/line-overflow adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust wording to accommodate slugline/line length so overflow does not spoil line breaks (example: 'Ellington' longer than 'Elon' required shortening a subsequent line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a place-name or word is longer than expected and would overload a line, shorten adjacent lines (or adjust wording) to absorb the overflow while allowing later lines to remain unchanged; be mindful of compositors' line limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know local specialties (not just 'big four')
rubrics_metrics.description: The sports editor assumes that an applicant knows the usual sports and looks for the man familiar with the one or two specialties popular in his city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond football, baseball, basketball, and boxing, develop knowledge of the sports that matter in the specific town (hockey in one town, polo in another). Editors value specialties; tailor your expertise to local tastes rather than only the national sports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop broad specialty to build readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Burt's best escape will be to develop some reasonably broad specialty, such as high-school sports. Many a paper puts one man on the high schools and has him follow them from football through baseball.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a specialty that attracts a steady local readership (e.g., high-school sports) to increase your value to the paper and raise your market price; this can be a quicker path to recognition than general wire-copy work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a wide and varied audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports must be written for a wide and varied audience. This involves a study of the individual city, for what is popular in one town may be uninteresting in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance content to appeal to different reader groups (players, watchers, school children, parents, women). Consider metropolis versus small city differences: metropolitan readers are mostly watchers; small-city readers are often participants and want local coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to radio by emphasizing analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports have reacted to the radio. The newspaper story, accordingly, tends to concentrate the play-by-play to the few moments that determined the outcome and to give much of its space to analysis and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since radio provides play-by-play, compress recitation of every play and focus on interpretation of decisive moments, causes, and the 'how' behind plays rather than pure chronological narration of actions the audience already knows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department ethics: no paid promotions or outside money
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports-department ethics are catching up with those in the rest of the paper. The reporter who writes promotional puff pieces for money is in poor position ethically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept money from promoters or act as a publicity agent for events you cover. Maintain independence so you can critique events honestly; accepting payments undermines credibility and can lead to dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle gambling pools cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: One problem remains largely unsolved: what to do about the gambling pools which have fostered such an interest in forecasts of victors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of abetting gambling by overemphasizing picks or running columns that function as betting guides. Seek ways to satisfy reader interest in forecasts without encouraging pool activity; be mindful of employer policies and community norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in clear English; avoid tired jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports can be written in English. The jargon that fills the sloppy sports page is a direct and traceable result of the reporter's weariness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived synonyms and grotesque vocabulary invented to escape repetition (e.g., 'sphere', 'horsehide', 'mischievous missile'). Use clear, natural language that readers can follow; don't sacrifice clarity for novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalizing blood and gore in conflict sports
rubrics_metrics.description: The conflict sports, such as boxing and wrestling, are hurt rather than helped by emphasis upon blood and battering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist writing aimed solely at attracting spectators hoping to see someone hurt. Many papers have outgrown gore stories; choose respectful coverage that does not glorify violence unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect amateur athletes; don't sneer
rubrics_metrics.description: The decline of sneering at amateurs. Sports writers are realizing that the amateur ... isn't to be judged by the same inflexible standards as is the professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cruel characterizations of amateur players who lack experience; contextualize mistakes and steer clear of unnecessarily harsh language toward high-school or amateur performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overemphasis on victory; apply the law of averages
rubrics_metrics.description: Overemphasis upon victory. The law of averages dictates that a team should lose half its games ... To some writers a team defeated is a team disgraced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat every loss as disgrace; avoid inflaming reader demand for scapegoats. Provide balanced perspective rather than sensationalizing failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate coach and team in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Slim progress has been made in differentiating between the coach and the team. The Terriers are the Sandersonmen ... If the team wins, the coach gets the glory; if the team loses, he gets the condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic attributions of team performance solely to coaching; analyze systemic factors and performance rather than reflexively calling for firings or blaming individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant wartime/military metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Let's leave the war to the front pages and quit using military expressions in football copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overuse military vocabulary (e.g., 'torpedoed','salient','blitzkrieg') in sports stories; readers often seek sports pages as an escape from war coverage and military metaphors become stale when overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core requirements: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing sports news involves four main points: (i) Accuracy; ... Enough readers saw the game and enough know so much about the sport that an erroneous statement will be spotted at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know officials' signals, keep proper box scores, and verify figures and facts. Avoid guesses about officiating or scoring details; readers will catch errors quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core requirements: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness means, in effect, 'don't turn a defeat for the home team into a "moral victory."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report honestly without local bias or excuses; don't attribute visitor losses solely to bad luck or officiating unless evidenced. Balance coverage so readers trust impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core requirements: Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis is the newspaper's best way of catching up with the radio's spot story, but analysis is far more than random guessing. It is built upon unremitting attention to the details of the game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base analysis on meticulous observation and selective detail-gathering. Explain how plays developed and why outcomes occurred rather than relying on flashy but shallow labels ('sudden, unexpected air attack').

rubrics_metrics.name: Core requirements: Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure demands planning a story so that the readers can anticipate what is coming next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the story (lead, secondary lead, running story, box score) so summaries and details align; ensure the summary accounts for all key items later elaborated in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead material options (five possibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead has five possibilities for material. It is a summary intended for the casual reader ... The five possibilities are: 1. How the scores were made and by whom; 2. A tie-in between result and features which produced that result; 3. A comparison of the teams and players; 4. A focusing upon the stars; 5. A picture of the crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the lead style that best hooks casual readers: summarise scoring, link result to causal features, compare teams, highlight star performers with explanation, or paint the crowd/setting. Secondary leads can follow if more than one item is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running story (detailed account) conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The running story is the 'detailed account,' already forecast in the lead. It is narrative and chronological ... Usually each play is described in a single sentence, for the benefit of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the running story in chronological narrative, using mostly single-sentence play descriptions for clarity, vary sentence length when plays require longer treatment, and establish a significance threshold so only plays meriting mention are included when space is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set a significance standard when space limits play descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the running story does not permit describing every play, the reporter must establish a standard for judging how significant a play must be to receive mention. This requires allotting his space logically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plays by impact on outcome or demonstration of key themes; avoid uneven coverage that details early plays heavily but rushes the decisive final quarter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box score rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The final element is the table or box score, about which there are two injunctions: (i) make sure the score adds correctly; (2) follow the paper's style sheet meticulously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check arithmetic in box scores and adhere strictly to the newspaper's style sheet on placement and format of errors, hits, runs, put-outs, etc. Consider compositor workload: avoid adding unexpected columns that require retrimming and extra typesetting time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-block structure (lead & secondary lead arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story structure often resolves into the familiar 'lead and secondary lead' arrangement which divides into blocks (examples provided for a multi-fight boxing program: Block 1 lead, Block 2 secondary lead, Block 3 catch-all, Block 4 elaboration of the lead, Block 5 elaboration of the secondary lead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize stories into logical blocks: start with the lead (principal result and decisive moments), provide a compact secondary lead for other important items, include a catch-all for notices and upcoming events, then elaborate the lead and secondary lead in sequence for narrative clarity.
